title: Leave the hollyhock up
translation: When the Kamo Festival was over, someone had all the hollyhock leaves taken down from the blinds, saying they weren't needed any more. I thought it was rather dull of them. But this was a person of taste, so I wondered whether there was some rule I didn't know about. Then I thought of a poem by Suō no Naishi:

Hung up for nothing,
the hollyhock on the blind,
"the day we meet":
we don't see each other now,
and its leaves have dried.

Her collection says she wrote it about the dry hollyhock leaves hanging on the blinds of the main hall. An old poem has a note saying it was "sent tied to a withered hollyhock". Sei Shōnagon puts "a dried hollyhock" on her list of things that make you miss the past, and that was a lovely thing to notice. And Kamo no Chōmei wrote in his book of the seasons: "On the jewelled blind, the hollyhock stays on after the festival."
It's sad enough when they wither by themselves. Why tear them down and leave nothing?

The herb balls hung on the curtained bed at the iris festival in early summer are replaced with chrysanthemums at the chrysanthemum festival in autumn, they say. So the irises in them should stay up until then. After the Empress Dowager of the Biwa Palace died, Ben no Menoto found dry irises and herb balls still hanging inside her old curtained bed, and wrote: "and still I hang the roots, though their time is past". And Gō no Jijū wrote back: "The irises are still here."

literal: Since the festival was over, saying the hollyhock afterwards was not needed, a certain person had all of it on the blinds taken down, and it seemed to me lacking in charm, but since it was what a person of quality did, I thought perhaps it was proper, yet Suō no Naishi
'Though I hang it (though I set my heart on it), what is in vain is, for both of us, the withered leaves of the hollyhock (the day of meeting) on the blind (not seeing)'
composed, and it is written in her house collection that she composed it about withered hollyhock leaves hanging on the blinds of the main hall.
In the headnote of an old poem, too, there is 'sent attached to a withered hollyhock'.
That in the Pillow Book, too, she wrote 'Things that make one long for the past: withered hollyhock': that was a very endearing thing to think of.
In Kamo no Chōmei's Four Seasons Tale, too, it is written: 'On the jewelled blind the hollyhock remains afterwards.'
Even their withering by themselves is (sad) enough; how should one take them away and throw them out without a trace?
Since they say the herb balls hung on the curtained dais are also exchanged for chrysanthemums on the ninth day of the ninth month, the irises should surely stay until the time of the chrysanthemums.

After the Empress Dowager of Biwa passed away, seeing withered irises, herb balls and the like still in her old curtained dais, Ben no Menoto said, 'still I hang the roots out of season', and in reply to that, Gō no Jijū composed, 'the iris grass remains'.

notes.quote: 祭過ぎぬれば、後の葵不用なりとて
notes.text: The Kamo Festival in the fourth month, today's Aoi Matsuri (see section 137). For the festival, hollyhock leaves ({葵|あふひ}) were hung on blinds, pillars and carriages. The question here is whether to take them down as soon as it is over.
{色|いろ} here is 'charm, feeling' (the 1925 edition: 'tasteless'), not 'colour'.
Suō no Naishi, a lady-in-waiting and poet of the late eleventh century, named after her father's post as governor of Suō. One of her poems is in the Hundred Poets anthology (Hyakunin Isshu).

notes.quote: かくれどもかひなき物はもろともにみすの葵の枯葉なりけり
notes.text: A poem built on puns (the 1925 edition lists them): かく is 'to hang' and 'to set your heart on'; みす is {御簾|みす} 'blind' and {見|み}ず 'not seeing'; あふひ is {葵|あふひ} 'hollyhock' and {逢|あ}ふ{日|ひ} 'the day of meeting'; {枯|か}れ 'withered' sounds like {離|か}れ 'drifting apart'. The leaves on the blind are also two lovers who no longer meet.
A poet's personal collection of poems ({家集|かしふ}), often with notes on when and why each poem was written.

notes.quote: 来しかた恋しきもの。かれたる葵。
notes.text: From one of Sei Shōnagon's lists in the Pillow Book: 'Things that make you miss the past'. Dried hollyhock is the first item. Kenkō quotes the heading slightly differently from the usual text.

Kamo no Chōmei (died 1216), the author of the Hōjōki, was from a family of priests of the Kamo Shrine. The Four Seasons Tale went under his name, but scholars doubt that he wrote it. The 1925 edition gives the whole poem the line comes from, 'On the jewelled blind the hollyhock stays on; even withered, let it bring back the face I love', and attributes it to Izumi Shikibu.

notes.quote: 己と枯るるだにこそあるを
notes.text: だに … を: 'even just (this) is (sad enough), and yet…'. The thing left unsaid, 'sad enough', is the point.

{薬玉|くすだま}: a ball of fragrant herbs and irises with long coloured threads, hung up on the fifth day of the fifth month to keep illness away. On the ninth day of the ninth month it was replaced with chrysanthemums. {御帳|みちやう}: the curtained platform in a noble's room, used as a bed and a seat. Modern くす{玉|だま}, the paper ball that is split open at ceremonies, takes its name from it.

Fujiwara no Kenshi (994–1027), a daughter of Michinaga and consort of Emperor Sanjō, named after her Biwa palace. After her death, Ben no Menoto wrote: 'irises: I have restrung them with the jewels of my tears, and still I hang the roots, though their time is past' (ね is both 'root' and 'the sound of weeping'). Gō no Jijū answered: 'the irises we strung are still here; did I ever think her bedroom would be left to ruin?' The 1925 edition gives both poems in full and places them in the imperial anthology Senzaishū. It reads 江 as え; she is usually called Gō no Jijū (がう).
